subject: English
passage: The National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) tracks changes in cognitive function among 15,000 elderly Americans over extended periods. As is true of most longitudinal research, this requirement for years of data collection results in substantial costs. By contrast, a relatively simple consumer preference study, such as one that is merely trying to determine what percentage of smartphone users in a city prefer touchscreen keyboards over physical ones, may not need a large budget because ______
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: longitudinal approaches are probably appropriate for the consumer preference study.
choices.B: it would be simple for NHATS researchers to include additional questions in their cognitive function study.
choices.C: 15,000 participants is more than sufficient for NHATS to detect changes in cognitive function.
choices.D: the consumer preference study can be completed effectively without years of data collection.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it most logically completes the text's discussion of the costs of different research approaches. The text indicates that NHATS is a longitudinal study—it involves tracking changes over extended time periods—and that the "requirement for years of data collection" is what causes it and most other longitudinal research to have substantial costs. The text then contrasts such studies with simpler studies, using the example of a consumer preference study that wants only to find out what percentage of smartphone users in a particular location prefer one keyboard type over another, that may not demand a large budget. The contrast emphasized in the text most directly suggests that the consumer preference study may cost less than a study like NHATS because the preference study aims only to determine current preferences and thus can be completed effectively without extending data collection over years.

Why C is incorrect:

Choice C is incorrect because the idea that NHATS involves more participants than necessary would be relevant to the costs of that research but would be completely irrelevant as an explanation for why an unrelated consumer preference study may not need a large budget; the studies have no direct bearing on each other.
